title: As-Sami', the All-Hearing
hook: the All-Hearing, who hears every whisper
tomorrow: if God is always watching, is that a threat or a comfort?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Mudhill, the one who humbles, and Qarun's ground opening. The line: status passes. Today, a woman nobody important was listening to.

Voice memos you never sent. A draft text that says everything, sitting unsent since last night. Most of what people say never reaches anyone. So here's an odd detail. One surah of the Qur'an is named for an argument. Al-Mujadilah: she who disputes. Its very first word is a verb, and the verb is heard. Yesterday's question was why a surah would be named for a woman arguing. The answer starts in a small room, with a woman pleading about her marriage, and someone sitting in the corner who can't make out all her words.
screen: `THE UNSENT TEXT.` → `A SURAH NAMED FOR AN ARGUMENT.` → `ITS FIRST WORD: HEARD.`

segments.voice: Tradition names her Khawlah. Her husband had sworn an old oath that cut her off as a wife, and she came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to plead her case, again and again. Then the surah opens, in Pickthall's words: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee." Her complaint goes into scripture, and the verses after it undo that oath's hold. Here's the part to tell a friend tonight. In a hadith, Aisha says she was in the same room, and she could not hear some of what the woman said. Glory to the one whose hearing takes in every voice, she said. The person a few feet away missed it. The verse says Allah heard it all. That's As-Sami', the All-Hearing. Not a speaker turned up loud. In another hadith, when people were shouting their praise on a journey, the Prophet told them to go easy on themselves: you aren't calling on someone deaf or far away. So the puzzle solves itself. The surah carries her name because she argued, and because her argument was heard. A whisper reaches. A complaint brought to Him is not a lack of faith; it's the opening line of a surah.
screen: `A WOMAN PLEADS HER CASE.` · `ALLAH HATH HEARD.` · `AISHA, A FEW FEET AWAY, MISSED IT.` · `NOT DEAF, NOT FAR AWAY.` · then, large: `HEARD.`

segments.voice: Bring your voice down to almost nothing, lips barely moving. If you pray, whisper a du'a in your own words about the thing you haven't told anyone. Or simply whisper that thing once, into the quiet, and let the sit hold the silence after it.
screen: `VOICE DOWN TO A WHISPER.` · `THE THING YOU HAVEN'T SAID.`

segments.voice: As-Sami'. The All-Hearing, who caught every word of a complaint that the person in the corner missed.
The line to keep: heard, every whisper, even the ones that never reach a phone. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims make du'a aloud or in a whisper, in Arabic or any language, at any time; the Qur'an's Surah al-Mujadilah opens with Allah hearing a woman's complaint.

original.note: Arabic: the All-Hearing. Surah al-Mujadilah opens with its verb: heard.

trapdoor: what you thought: God hears like a very big microphone.
what it means: nothing said, even in a whisper, goes unheard, and a complaint brought to Him is welcome.
what a scholar hears: Surah 58 takes its name from 58:1; tradition names the woman Khawlah bint Tha'labah; the ruling on her husband's oath (zihar) follows in 58:2–4.

the one who hears the loudest voice first

chat.meaning: As-Sami' hears every whisper, and a woman's complaint opens a surah. A hurt can be brought to Him before it goes anywhere else.
